claim: Heart disease is a major cause of mortality.
source: Heart diseases is a major cause of mortality (Bezzina et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bezzina et al., 2015

claim: Hundreds of genetic variants related to cardiovascular traits have been identified by genome-wide association studies.
source: Although a large number of genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of genetic variants related to cardiovascular traits (Roselli et al., 2018; van Setten et al., 2018; Shah et al., 2020; Verweij et al., 2020), we are very far from a comprehensive understanding of the genetic architecture of these complex traits.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published GWAS studies

claim: Orthologous genes control the early development and essential functional elements of the heart from flies to mammals.
source: Indeed, orthologous genes control the early development as well as the essential functional elements of the heart.
evidence: Draws from established scientific consensus about evolutionary conservation of cardiac genes

claim: The fly is the simplest genetic model with a heart muscle.
source: The fly is the simplest genetic model with a heart muscle and is increasingly used to identify the genes involved in heart disease and aging (Ocorr et al., 2007b; Diop and Bodmer, 2015; Rosenthal et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Wild populations of flies harbor rare polymorphisms of major effects that predispose them to cardiac dysfunction.
source: We previously showed that wild populations of flies harbor rare polymorphisms of major effects that predispose them to cardiac dysfunction (Ocorr et al., 2007a).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: The DGRP is a community resource of sequenced inbred lines.
source: For this, we used the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) (Mackay et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2014), a community resource of sequenced inbred lines.
evidence: Supported by citations describing the DGRP resource

claim: Inheritance of most quantitative traits in Drosophila is complex, involving many genes with small additive effects as well as epistatic interactions.
source: Previous GWAS performed in the DGRP indicate that inheritance of most quantitative traits in Drosophila is complex, involving many genes with small additive effects as well as epistatic interactions (Mackay and Huang, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mackay and Huang, 2018

claim: 167 lines from the DGRP were measured for heart parameters in 1-week-old females.
source: To assess the magnitude of naturally occurring variations of the traits, we measured heart parameters in 1-week-old females for 167 lines from the DGRP, a publicly available population of sequenced inbred lines derived from wild caught females (Figure 1A).
evidence: Describes the experimental design and sample size used in the study

claim: Fly cardiac function parameters are highly influenced by sex.
source: Fly cardiac function parameters are highly influenced by sex (Wessells et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wessells et al., 2004

claim: A total sample of 1956 individuals was analyzed for cardiac traits.
source: A total sample of 1956 individuals was analyzed.
evidence: Reports the total number of individuals analyzed in the study

claim: Seven cardiac traits were analyzed across the whole population.
source: Seven cardiac traits were analyzed across the whole population (Figure 1—source data 1 and Table 1).
evidence: Describes the number of cardiac traits measured in the study

claim: Significant genetic variation was found for all cardiac traits.
source: We found significant genetic variation for all traits (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) with broad sense heritability ranging from 0.30 (AI) to 0.56 (EDD) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in figures and table showing heritability estimates

claim: Broad sense heritability for cardiac traits ranged from 0.30 (AI) to 0.56 (EDD).
source: We found significant genetic variation for all traits (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) with broad sense heritability ranging from 0.30 (AI) to 0.56 (EDD) (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by heritability calculations presented in Table 1

claim: Quantitative cardiac traits were poorly correlated with each other except for EDD/ESD and HP/DI.
source: Except for EDD/ESD and HP/DI, quantitative traits were poorly correlated with each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: GWAS analyses were performed using a linear mixed model accounting for effects of Wolbachia infection and common polymorphism inversions.
source: To identify candidate variants associated with cardiac performance variation, we performed GWAS analyses and evaluated single marker associations of line means with common variants using a linear mixed model (Lippert et al., 2011) and after accounting for effects of Wolbachia infection and common polymorphism inversions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Describes the statistical method and covariates used in GWAS analysis

claim: None of the variants reached the strict Bonferroni correction threshold for multiple tests (2 · 10–8).
source: For most of the phenotypes analyzed, quantile-quantile (QQ) plots were uniform (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and none of the variants reached the strict Bonferroni correction threshold for multiple tests (2 · 10–8), which is usual in the DGRP given the size of the population.
evidence: Reports the statistical significance threshold and that no variants reached it

claim: The top 100 ranked variants for each quantitative trait were selected for analysis.
source: We therefore chose to analyze the 100 top ranked variants for each quantitative trait.
evidence: Describes the selection criteria for variants to be analyzed further

claim: 530 unique variants were identified among the seven quantitative traits analyzed.
source: Among the seven quantitative traits analyzed, we identified 530 unique variants.
evidence: Reports the total number of unique variants identified across all traits

claim: 417 variants were mapped to 332 genes.
source: Using these criteria, 417 variants were mapped to 332 genes (Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: Reports the number of variants mapped to genes using specified criteria

claim: Genomic locations of the variants were biased toward regions within 1 kb upstream of genes TSS.
source: Genomic locations of the variants were biased toward regions within 1 kb upstream of genes TSS, and, to a lesser extent, to genes 5' UTR (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by chi-squared test results shown in Figure 1C

claim: 288 unique SNPs were identified through epistasis analysis, which were mapped to 261 genes.
source: FastEpistasis reports best ranked interacting SNP for each starting focal SNP, thus extending the network of variants and genes associated to natural variation of cardiac performance, which were used for hypothesis generation and functional validations; 288 unique SNPs were identified, which were mapped to 261 genes (Figure 1—source data 3, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Reports the results of epistasis analysis

claim: There is a significant overlap between the 332 genes associated with single marker GWAS and the 261 genes identified by epistasis (n=31).
source: While none of the focal SNPs interacted with each other, there is a significant overlap between the 332 genes associated with single marker GWAS and the 261 genes identified by epistasis (n=31, Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1e, fold change (FC)=6; hypergeometric pval=6.8 × 10–16).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing significant overlap with hypergeometric p-value

claim: Single marker GWAS and epistatic interactions identified a compendium of 562 genes associated with natural variations of heart performance.
source: Taken together, single marker GWAS and epistatic interactions performed on the seven cardiac phenotypes identified a compendium of 562 genes associated with natural variations of heart performance (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Reports the total number of genes identified across all analyses

claim: Genes encoding signaling receptors, TFs, and cell adhesion molecules were over-represented among the gene sets associated with cardiac performance.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the combined single marker GWAS and epistatic interactions analyses indicated that genes encoding signaling receptors, TFs, and cell adhesion molecules were over-represented among these gene sets (pval=1.4 × 10–9 [FC=2.9], 5×10–4 [FC=2], and 3×10–3 [FC=4.6], respectively).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis with reported p-values and fold changes

claim: There was a bias for genes encoding proteins located at the plasma membrane, at ion channel complexes, and components of contractile fibers.
source: There was also a bias for genes encoding proteins located at the plasma membrane, at ion channel complexes as well as components of contractile fibers (pval=3.4 × 10–10 [FC=3], 7×10–5 [FC=4.2], and 4×10–2 [FC=3.6]; Figure 2A; Supplementary file 2a).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis with reported p-values and fold changes

claim: Genes identified in a global screen for stress-induced lethality following heart-specific RNAi KD were not enriched in GWAS detected genes.
source: In addition, genes identified in a global screen for stress-induced lethality following heart-specific RNAi KD (Neely et al., 2010) were also not enriched in GWAS detected genes (FC=1; Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing GWAS genes to previously identified genes

claim: Genes associated to natural variations of cardiac traits are typically missed by traditional forward or reverse genetics approaches.
source: This indicates that genes associated to natural variations of cardiac traits are typically missed by traditional forward or reverse genetics approaches, which highlights the value of our approach.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of enrichment for genes identified by traditional genetic approaches

claim: 148 of the GWAS identified genes were directly connected within the fly interactome and formed a large network of interacting genes/proteins.
source: Remarkably, a high proportion (148) of the GWAS identified genes were directly connected within the fly interactome and formed a large network of interacting genes/proteins (Supplementary file 2c and d, Figure 2B), suggesting that they participate in common biological processes.
evidence: Supported by network analysis showing direct connections between GWAS genes

claim: 38 of 42 selected genes tested led to significant effects on cardiac performance traits upon heart-specific RNAi knockdown.
source: Notably, 38 of the 42 selected genes led to various levels of cardiac performance defects following heart-specific KD (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Genes selected from GWAS lead to significantly more frequent cardiac phenotypes when inactivated in the heart compared to randomly selected genes.
source: Although a number of these genes lead to cardiac phenotypes when inactivated – which is consistent with published observations that quantitative traits can be influenced by a large number of genes (Zhang et al., 2021) – when inactivated in the heart, the genes selected from GWAS lead to significantly more frequent phenotypes compared to the randomly selected genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of GWAS-selected genes to randomly selected genes

claim: snooBSC234/sogUU2 double heterozygotes flies showed non-additive SI phenotypes, suggesting a genetic interaction.
source: Importantly, compared to each single heterozygotes, snooBSC234/sogUU2 double heterozygotes flies showed non-additive SI phenotypes (two-way ANOVA pval: 2.1 · 10–7), suggesting a genetic interaction (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA statistical analysis of genetic interaction

claim: babo/tkv heterozygotes displayed non-additive ESD and EDD phenotypes.
source: We thus tested other allelic combinations for loss of function alleles of BMP and activin pathways. babo/tkv heterozygotes (respectively activin and BMP type 1 receptors) displayed non-additive ESD and EDD phenotypes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing non-additive effects

claim: mad/smox heterozygotes displayed non-additive effects on several traits, including phenotypes related to rhythmicity (HP, SI, DI) and contractility (ESD and EDD).
source: In addition, mad/smox heterozygotes (specifc downstream TFs of BMP and activin pathways) displayed non-additive effects on several traits, including phenotypes related to rhythmicity (HP, SI, DI) and contractility (ESD and EDD) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing non-additive effects

claim: 95% of variants were localized in non-coding regions of the genome.
source: In addition, most variants (95%) were localized in non-coding regions of the genome.
evidence: Reports the proportion of variants in non-coding regions

claim: The distribution of variants was enriched in gene proximal (0–1 kb) upstream regions.
source: Remarkably, their distribution was enriched in gene proximal (0–1 kb) upstream regions (Figure 1C) suggesting that a high proportion of variants affects cis-regulatory sequences.
evidence: Supported by chi-squared test results shown in Figure 1C

claim: Oligo analysis of the 150 bp sequences around non-coding variants detected significant over-represented k-mers.
source: However, oligo analysis (van Helden et al., 1998) of the 150 bp sequences around these non-coding variants detected significant over-represented k-mers (Evalue ≤ 1e-4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis of sequences around variants

claim: DNA binding motifs for TFs that were themselves associated with natural variations of the cardiac traits were identified.
source: Remarkably, we identified DNA binding motifs for TFs that were themselves associated with natural variations of the cardiac traits. Some examples are klumpfuss (klu/ZBTB7A), luna (KLF5-7), longitudinals lacking (lola/BTB18), serpent (srp/GATA1-6), mirror (mirr/IRX3-6), Helix Loop Helix protein 3B (HLH3B/TAL2), and defective proventiculus (dve/SATB1) which were also identified by GWAS (see Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis and comparison with GWAS results

claim: All tested TFs (luna, lola, srp, mirr, mad, klu, and HLH3B) are associated with changes in multiple cardiac traits upon heart-specific knockdown.
source: As illustrated in Figure 3C, all tested TFs are associated with changes in multiple cardiac traits.
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 3C

claim: The Levene test found evidence of significant heterogeneity among the lines in the variance for all analyzed cardiac traits.
source: We used the Levene test Levene, 1960 to examine heterogeneity of the 'micro-environmental' variance among lines for the seven analyzed cardiac traits. We found evidence of significant heterogeneity among the lines in the variance for all analyzed cardiac traits (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by Levene test statistical analysis reported in Table 1

claim: Significant genetic variation was found for all CVe traits.
source: We found significant genetic variation for all CVe traits (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) indicating that within some lines, individuals display relatively constant cardiac performance traits, whereas within others, individuals display widely varying cardiac traits.
evidence: Supported by data presented in figures showing variation in CVe traits

claim: CVe traits were poorly correlated with each other, except for HP/DI and EDD/ESD.
source: Similar to trait means, CVe traits were poorly correlated with each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), except for HP/DI and EDD/ESD.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Correlations of CVe traits with their respective trait means ranged from moderate (FS: –0.53) to none (DI: 0.064, SI: 0.09, ESD: 0.08).
source: Correlations of CVe traits with their respective trait means ranged from moderate (FS: –0.53) to none (DI: 0.064, SI: 0.09, ESD: 0.08) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: GWAS analysis on CVe traits identified 887 variants and 566 genes associated with natural variations of CVe of cardiac performance.
source: Overall, this led to the identification of 887 variants and 566 genes associated with natural variations of CVe of cardiac performance (Figure 4—source data 1, Supplementary file 3a), which were used for hypothesis generation and functional annotations.
evidence: Reports the results of GWAS analysis on CVe traits

claim: Only three variants were associated with both trait means and CVe.
source: Consistent with the weak correlation between cardiac trait CVe and trait means, we found only three variants associated with both (Figure 4C and D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2; Supplementary file 3c).
evidence: Supported by comparison of GWAS results for means and CVe

claim: Among 566 genes detected from trait CVe and 562 genes detected by trait mean GWAS, 92 genes are found associated with both.
source: Among 566 detected respectively from trait CVe and 562 genes detected by trait mean GWAS, 92 genes are found associated with both (FC=5, hypergeometric pval=2.2 × 10–39).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis showing significant overlap with hypergeometric p-value

claim: Within the CVe-associated genes there was an over-representation of cell adhesion processes, transmembrane signaling, and ion channel activity.
source: Within the CVe-associated genes we observed an over-representation of cell adhesion processes, transmembrane signaling, and ion channel activity (pval=1.6 × 10–8 (FC=7), 1.1×10–3 (FC=2,2), and 4.5×10–2 (FC=2,5) respectively).
evidence: Supported by GO enrichment analysis with reported p-values and fold changes

claim: Genes leading to stress-induced lethality upon heart-specific KD were significantly under-represented in the CVe gene set.
source: In addition, genes leading to stress-induced lethality upon heart-specific KD (Neely et al., 2010) were significantly under-represented in this gene set (FC=0,6; p=0,05; Supplementary file 3e).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing CVe genes to previously identified genes

claim: Variants localized in the proximal region of the genes (0–1 kb upstream of TSS) are over-represented among SNPs associated with traits CVe.
source: As for trait means, variants localized in the proximal region of the genes (0–1 kb upstream of TSS) are over-represented among SNPs associated with traits CVe (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by chi-squared test results shown in Figure 4E

claim: Both sets of GWAS-associated genes were significantly enriched for genes that have a human orthologue compared to the whole fly genome gene set.
source: Compared to the whole fly genome gene set (17,500 genes), both sets of GWAS-associated genes were significantly enriched for genes that have a human orthologue (FC = 1.4, pval = 4.3 · 10–21 for genes associated with trait means and FC = 1.25; pval = 7 · 10–11 for genes associated with traits CVe, Table 2), indicating that, overall, the loci associated with natural variations in cardiac traits have evolutionary conserved functions.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing GWAS genes to whole genome

claim: GWAS loci were enriched for genes whose human orthologues were associated with cardiac disorders.
source: More importantly, GWAS loci were enriched for genes whose human orthologues were associated with cardiac disorders (FC = 1.66 [trait means] and 1.7 [traits CVe], pval = 7 · 10–6, Table 2 and Supplementary file 4b and e).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis comparing fly GWAS genes to human cardiac disorder genes

claim: Heart-specific knockdown of poxm/PAX9 and sr/EGR2 induced an increased heart rate in flies.
source: We first tested the effects of heart-specific KD on cardiac performance in flies using the in vivo assay. Both induced an increased heart rate (reduced HP and SI; Figure 5A) but did not affect other cardiac traits analyzed (not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of both PAX9 and EGR2 induced shortening of the AP duration in hiPSC-CMs.
source: As shown in Figure 5C–E, both gene KDs induced shortening of the AP duration, thus suggesting conserved function in setting cardiac rhythm for both TFs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-E

claim: The effect of PAX9 KD on AP duration was stronger and seems specific to the repolarization phase, as suggested by APD50 and 75 shortening.
source: The effect was stronger for PAX9 KD and seems specific to the repolarization phase, as suggested by APD50 and 75 shortening (Figure 5F–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F-I

claim: APD shortening for PAX9 KD was coincident with increased expression of Na+ and K+ ion channels (SCN5A, KCNH2, and KNCQ1).
source: APD shortening for PAX9 KD was coincident with increased expression of Na+ and K+ ion channels (SCN5A, KCNH2, and KNCQ1) (Figure 5J), supporting the APD shortening phenotype.
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5J

claim: Assessment of the PAX9 KD effect on sarcomeric content revealed an increase in sarcomeric gene expression.
source: Finally, assessment of the PAX9 KD effect on sarcomeric content revealed an increase in sarcomeric gene expression (Figure 5K), and an upregulation of genes associated with an hypertrophic response (NPPA, NPPB, and NPR1) (Battistoni et al., 2012), which was coincident with increased CM size as quantified by the area of TNNT2 staining per cardiac nuclei (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: Supported by gene expression and imaging data shown in Figure 5K-M

claim: PAX9 KD was coincident with increased CM size as quantified by the area of TNNT2 staining per cardiac nuclei.
source: Finally, assessment of the PAX9 KD effect on sarcomeric content revealed an increase in sarcomeric gene expression (Figure 5K), and an upregulation of genes associated with an hypertrophic response (NPPA, NPPB, and NPR1) (Battistoni et al., 2012), which was coincident with increased CM size as quantified by the area of TNNT2 staining per cardiac nuclei (Figure 5L and M).
evidence: Supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5L and M
